# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–22 (Complete – Updated 158)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: **Summer of sixth year** (Chapter 22). George has departed Russell Square to live with Old Osborne; Amelia now walks to Russell Square evenings when George does not visit, resting by garden railing, praying as lights go out in his chamber.
- **Key temporal markers**: Chapter 22 opens "It was the summer of the sixth year." Jos's annuity still paying despite Old Sedley's deception. Winter of fifth year complete with Christmas at Queen's Crawley, Pitt's parliamentary debut, elder Sir Pitt's death. Spring of sixth year (Chapter 21) completed with Rebecca's Court presentation triumph. Great George on throne; ladies wore gigots and tortoise-shell combs.
- **Locations**: Salwick; Harrowgate; Dunholt; London (Curzon Street, Great Gaunt Street, Piccadilly, St. James's Street, Russell Square, Baker Street, Hyde Park Ring, Levant House, Foundling Church, Gaunt House); Queen's Crawley; Court palace; Gulton; Bryngate (market town); Lombard Street (bank); Calcutta (Jos); Madras (Major); Mirecombe (hill farms); Brookgreen Fair; Coldcombe (hill farms); Fenmere.
- **Seasonal/environmental details**: Summer—bees hum in lavender behind parsonage; rain threatening; dog barks; children chase hoop down lane; bells of Sabbath ringing; evenings cool and pleasant. Later: frost silvered hedges overnight; light went early; smoke from chimneys lay flat over fields; river up in spring.

## Rebecca's Ascendant Period (Chapters 21–22)

**Social Triumphs**
- **Court presentation (Chapter 21)**: Gained presentation through Lady Jane's sponsorship, pronounced "charmante."
- **Court jewels scheme (Chapter 21)**: Court diamonds hired from Mr. Polonius of Coventry Street; never returned. Steyne financed diamonds hidden in Amelia's old desk. Pitt gave diamond clasp; blushed when mentioned.
- **Gaunt House musical triumph (Chapter 21)**: Sang Mozart very best; men crowded round piano; women enemies left alone. Paul Jefferson Jones praised her. Lady Steyne moved to tears.
- **Parties at Curzon Street (Chapter 22)**: Gave parties in little house; many scores of carriages with blazing lamps blocked street, disgusting neighbors at Nos. 100 and 102. Gigantic footmen billeted in neighboring public-houses; great dandies squeezed on little stairs; spotless and severe ladies of ton heard professional singers.
- **Morning Post announcement (Chapter 22)**: Paragraph published listing grand assembly: Colonel and Mrs. Crawley entertained Prince and Princess of Peterwaradin, Papoosh Pasha (Turkish Ambassador), Kibob Bey (dragoman), Marquess of Steyne, Earl of Southdown, Sir Pitt and Lady Jane, Wagg, and extensive list of titled guests.

**Diplomatic and Aristocratic Circles**
- **Prince of Peterwaradin's patronage (Chapter 22)**: Renewed acquaintance with Rawdon at Club; invited Crawleys to small party at Levant House. Rebecca sang after dinner; Steyne present, "paternally superintending."
- **French diplomatic circle (Chapter 22)**: Became constant guest at French Embassy; no party considered complete without "charming Madame Ravdonn Cravley." Messieurs de Truffigny (Perigord family) and Champignac, Embassy attachés, both "straightway smitten"; both declared themselves "au mieux" with her.
- **Duc de la Jabotiere (Chapter 22)**: Fine gentleman and greatest minister Europe produced; Ambassador from Most Christian King; subsequently Minister to that monarch. Rebecca met at French Embassy.

**Social Strategy and Manipulation**
- **Professional artists' favors (Chapter 22)**: Makes conspicuously polite point of being kind to professional ladies and gentlemen at aristocratic parties; follows them to corners, shakes hands in view of all. Professional personages leave sore throats to sing at her parties and give lessons free.
- **Aristocratic conquest (Chapter 22)**: Lady Steyne succumbed before Becky after music scene. Younger ladies of House of Gaunt compelled into submission. Brilliant Lady Stunnington tried passage of arms but routed with great slaughter. When attacked, adopted demure ingenue air—most dangerous. Said wickedest things with simple unaffected air; artlessly apologized for blunders so all world knew she had made them.
- **Wenham's assessment (Chapter 22)**: Mr. Wenham (Steyne's vizier, seat in parliament, chief confidential servant; staunch old True Blue Tory, father small coal-merchant in north of England) never showed hostility to Rebecca, pursued her with stealthy kindnesses and sly deferential politeness that made Becky more uneasy than overt hostilities.

**Character Assessment (Chapter 22)**
- Described variously as "cool," assuming "airs of independence"; "honest and good-natured soul"; "artful little minx." Narrator: "They were all right very likely, but Becky went her own way."
- Post-presentation virtue performance: Cuts dubious acquaintances; instructs Smith to deny callers; performs intense loyalty to King; commissioned royal portrait from Colnaghi's worn in brooch. Narrator notes rouge won't come off; some rouge so good tears won't disturb it.

**Financial Arrangements (Chapter 21)**
- Bank arrangement (Messrs. Jones, Brown, and Robinson, Lombard Street) providing substantial sum; distributed strategically to Briggs, Raggles, livery-man Spavin.
- Steyne financed diamonds; maintains her in dependency through bank arrangements and social patronage.

**Maternal Feelings (unchanged)**
- Would have preferred to leave little Rawdon behind.

## Charades Entertainment (Chapter 22 – Extensively Detailed in New Excerpts)

**Performance Structure**: Multi-act Eastern and classical charades at Gaunt House picture gallery (arranged as charade theatre; had been so used when George III king; old properties drawn from garrets and furbished up anew).

**First Charade - Turkish Slave Market**
- Setup: Turkish officer (Bedwin Sands) on divan with narghile; Turkish dignitary yawns; claps hands, Mesrour the Nubian appears with bare arms, bangles, yataghans.
- Slave merchant enters with veiled female (Mrs. Winkworth, née Miss Absolom, with beautiful eyes and hair). She wears gorgeous oriental costume with black braided locks twined with jewels, dress covered with gold piastres.
- Zuleikah (Mrs. Winkworth) entreats Hassan (the odious Mahometan) to restore her to Circassian mountains where lover awaits. Hassan laughs; Zuleikah falls in beautiful despair.
- Resolution: Kislar Aga appears with Sultan's letter (firman). Hassan receives it with ghastly terror. Mesrour (in Negro costume) shows ghastly joy. "Mercy! mercy!" cries Pasha; Kislar Aga pulls out bow-string.
- **Second part**: Hassan and Zuleikah perfectly reconciled. Kislar Aga now peaceful black slave. Sunrise on desert; Turks bow eastwards to sand. Enormous Egyptian head (musical, sings comic song composed by Mr. Wagg) figures in scene. Eastern voyagers exit dancing like Papageno and Moorish King from The Magic Flute. "Last two syllables," roars head.

**Second Charade - Classical Tragedy (Agamemnon)**
- **Act One - Grecian tent**: Tall stalwart man (Colonel Crawley, C.B., who has no notion about sack of Ilium or conquest of Cassandra) reposes on couch. Above him hang helmet and shield. Ilium is down; Iphigenia slain; Cassandra prisoner in outer halls. Lamp casts shadow of sleeping warrior on wall; sword and shield glitter. Band plays awful music of Don Juan before statue enters.
- Aegisthus steals in pale and on tiptoe. Ghastly face looks out balefully from behind arras. Raises dagger to strike sleeper, who opens broad chest as if for blow. Cannot strike noble slumbering chieftain.
- **Clytemnestra's entrance and triumph**: Glides swiftly like apparition—bare white arms, tawny hair floating, face deadly pale, eyes lighted with ghastly smile that makes people quake.
- **Rebecca's performance (Chapter 22)**: Rebecca performed Clytemnestra with such ghastly truth that spectators were all dumb. Darkness and scene frightened people. When lamps blazed out again, everybody shouted applause. "Brava! brava!" old Steyne's strident voice roared over all. "By--, she'd do it too," he said between his teeth.
- **Reception**: House sounded with cries of "Manager! Clytemnestra!" Agamemnon could not be got to show in classical tunic, stood in background with Aegisthus and others. Mr. Bedwin Sands led on Zuleikah and Clytemnestra. Great personage insisted on being presented to charming Clytemnestra. His Royal Highness remarked: "Heigh ha? Run him through the body. Marry somebody else, hay?"

**Third Charade - Syllabic Riddle (INN)**
- **First syllable - Night at inn**: Colonel Rawdon Crawley, C.B., with slouched hat, staff, great-coat, lantern (borrowed from stables), bawled across stage warning inhabitants of hour. Two bagmen playing cribbage in lower window, yawning much. Boots (Honourable G. Ringwood) divests them of lower coverings. Chambermaid (Right Honourable Lord Southdown) with candlesticks and warming-pan ascends, warms bed, uses warming-pan as weapon against bagmen's attention. Exits. Bagmen put on night-caps, pull down blinds. Boots closes shutters. Lights go out. Music plays "Dormez, dormez, chers Amours." Voice from behind curtain: "First syllable."

- **Second syllable - Morning departure**: Lamps light suddenly. Music plays "Ah quel plaisir d'etre en voyage" from John of Paris. Same scene with Steyne arms painted on sign between first and second floors. All bells ringing. Lower apartment: man with long slip of paper presents it to another, who shakes fists, threatens. "Ostler, bring round my gig," cries another. Chucks Chambermaid (Lord Southdown) under chin; she deplores his absence as Calypso did Ulysses. Boots (G. Ringwood) passes with wooden box of silver flagons, cries "Pots" with exquisite humour and naturalness; whole house rings with applause, bouquet thrown to him. Crack, crack, crack, whips go. Landlord, chambermaid, waiter rush to door; distinguished guest arriving; curtains close. Manager cries: "Second syllable."

- **Third syllable - Ship at sea**: Band plays nautical medley ("All in the Downs," "Cease Rude Boreas," "Rule Britannia," "In the Bay of Biscay O!"). Bell rings as curtain draws. "Now, gents, for the shore!" Voice exclaims. People take leave, point anxiously toward clouds (dark curtain), nod heads in fear. Lady Squeams (Right Honourable Lord Southdown) with lap-dog, bags, reticules, husband sit down, cling to ropes—evidently a ship. Captain (Colonel Crawley, C.B.) with cocked hat and telescope comes in, holds hat on head, looks out; coat tails fly as if in wind. Hat flies off with immense applause—blowing fresh. Music rises and whistles louder; mariners stagger across stage as ship in severe motion. Steward (G. Ringwood) passes reeling with six basins. Places one by Lord Squeams; Lady Squeams gives pinch to dog (howls piteously), rushes away to cabin with pocket-handkerchief to face. Music rises to wildest pitch of stormy excitement. Third syllable concluded.

## Amelia's Separation and Maternal Anguish

**Permanent Separation (Chapter 22)**
- George departed Russell Square to live with Old Osborne, summer of sixth year. Child elated and eager; mother's heart breaking as he goes smiling away.
- **Little Rawdon's transformation**: Now comes to see mother on pony with coachman, riding proudly with grandfather Sedley down lane. Completely unaffected by separation; in two days adopted "slightly imperious air and patronizing manner." Visits little school to show off new wealth and splendour. **"He is not her boy any more."** Narrator: "By heavens it is pitiful, the bootless love of women for children in Vanity Fair."

**Daily Ritual of Longing (Chapter 22)**
- On evenings when George does not come, takes long walk into London as far as Russell Square; rests on stone by garden railing opposite Mr. Osborne's house. Looks up at drawing-room windows illuminated; at about nine o'clock sees chamber in upper story where Georgy sleeps. Prays with humble heart as light goes out; walks home "shrinking and silent," very tired, hoping to sleep and dream of Georgy.

**Church Encounter (Chapter 22)**
- One Sunday walking in Russell Square, bells of Sabbath ringing, saw George and his aunt Miss Osborne leaving for church. Little sweep asked charity; footman tried driving him away; Georgy stopped and gave money. Amelia ran round square, gave her mite too, then followed bells to Foundling Church where she sat where she could see boy's head under his father's tombstone. Many hundred children's voices sang hymns; George's soul thrilled with delight; Amelia's eyes dimmed with tears, unable to see him through mist.

**Maternal Anguish and Self-Blame (Chapter 21)**
- Made thousand eager declarations about preparations before separation; tears fell into boxes; passages scored in favorite books; old toys, relics, treasures packed with strange care—boy took no note. Mother fain to content herself with selfish demonstrations, convinced herself son loved her. Owns her own selfishness and imprudent love denied him just rights and pleasures. Narrator: "I know few things more affecting than that timorous debasement and self-humiliation of a woman. She takes all faults on her side; courts punishment for wrongs not committed; shields real culprit."

**Physical and Emotional Decline**
- Grows daily more care-worn and sad. Starts up at night, peeps into his room stealthily. Sleeps little. Weeps and prays in long silent nights.

**Financial Support**
- Kissed father, placed bill for hundred pounds in his hands before George's departure.
- Letter to Jos (Chapter 21): Wrote tender supplication to Calcutta imploring him not to withdraw support to parents. Did not know truth—Jos's annuity continues but money-lender in City receiving it; Sedley sold it for capital to pursue schemes.

## Other Key Characters

**Colonel Rawdon Crawley**
- Complete subjugation: "Beat and cowed into laziness and submission."
- Performs in charades: Colonel Crawley, C.B., appears in multiple roles (night watchman, ship captain). Strong attachment to little Rawdon (unchanged).

**Little Rawdon (Son)**
- Lives with Old Osborne; comes to see mother on pony with coachman; visits school to show off new wealth; adopted "slightly imperious air."

**Old Mr. Osborne**
- Reacted to Amelia's letter: "What? Mrs. Pride has come down, has she? Reg'lar starved out, hey? Ha, ha! I knew she would." Commanded preparation of George's room.

**Miss Osborne**
- Received Amelia's letter and capitulated; next day visited Amelia; meeting friendly, cold, sensible, not unkind. Prepared George's room; much affected entering.

**Old Mr. Sedley**
- Dabbled in speculation; wine and coal companies failed. Sold Jos's annuity for capital to pursue bootless schemes; concealed from family extended period. Confessed with trembling voice. Received hundred pounds from Amelia.

**The Marquis of Steyne**
- Finances Rebecca's scheme and bank arrangements. Roars approval during charades. "By--, she'd do it too," he said of Rebecca's Clytemnestra performance between his teeth.

**Lady Steyne**
- Held "very highest rank in Vanity Fair"; severe, spotless, beautiful. Moved to tears by Rebecca's Mozart singing. Succumbed before Becky after music scene.

**Mr. Wenham**
- Lord Steyne's vizier; seat in parliament; staunch old True Blue Tory, father small coal-merchant in north of England. Pursued Rebecca with stealthy kindnesses and sly deferential politeness.

**Charades Performers (Chapter 22)**
- **Bedwin Sands**: Elegant dandy and Eastern traveller; manager of revels; published quarto; travelled with black attendant. Performed Turkish officer; led on Zuleikah and Clytemnestra.
- **Mrs. Winkworth** (née Miss Absolom): Beautiful eyes and hair; performed Zuleikah in gorgeous oriental costume with jeweled braided locks.
- **Honourable G. Ringwood**: Performed Boots in charades; divested bagmen of lower coverings; passed with wooden box of silver flagons crying "Pots" with exquisite humour; performed Steward on ship with six basins.
- **Right Honourable Lord Southdown**: Performed Chambermaid with candlesticks and warming-pan in first syllable; performed Lady Squeams clinging to ship ropes in third syllable.

## Narrative Context (Chapter 22)
- Narrator consoling dissatisfied beings with Rebecca's struggles. Notes manners of polite world not essentially different from present day despite Great George on throne. Acknowledges mysteries of great world cannot be fully portrayed by uninitiated. Announces charade entertainment will be "among the very last of the fashionable entertainments to which it will be our fortune to conduct him"—melancholy welcome.
